sentences.text: Stagonolepis robertsoni was a quadruped approximately 3 meters long, covered in thick armored scales that ran along its body.
The front of its jaws lacked teeth and instead featured an upward-arching beak-like tip likely used to uproot plants similar to a modern pig.
Peg-like teeth at the back of its mouth were suitable for chewing tough vegetation like horsetails, ferns, and cycads.
The genus Stagonolepis was described by Louis Agassiz in 1844.
The type species of the genus is S. robertsoni, and S. olenkae was described in 2010.
As a slow-moving browser, it likely used its heavy armor to defend against attacks from carnivorous archosauriforms.
A 2018 paper suggested that the forelimb morphology of S. olenkae is an adaptation for scratch-digging.
Stagonolepis belongs to the family Stagonolepididae and is classified within the order Aetosauria.

Some paleontologists have considered the South American genus Aetosauroides to be a junior synonym of Stagonolepis, though most sequential studies conclude that Aetosauroides and Calyptosuchus are valid, monotypic genera distinct from Stagonolepis.
Stagonolepis fossils are found in the Carnian stage of the Late Triassic in Germany, Poland, and Scotland.
Stagonolepis is restricted to the Carnian stage of Scotland and Poland.
The time range for Stagonolepis is from the Carnian to the Norian stages, between 237 and 205.7 million years ago.
Some researchers question whether S. olenkae is a distinct species, suggesting it may be an example of intraspecific variety like sexual dimorphism.
